content: Sensory defensiveness is a condition characterized by an exaggerated or alarmed reaction to sensory input that is typically perceived as harmless or non-irritating by neurotypical individuals. While it is not uncommon for people to exhibit mild sensory defensive traits, the condition is diagnosed when multiple defensive traits significantly interfere with an individual’s daily life. Symptoms Common symptoms of sensory defensiveness include an intolerance to high-pitched noises, sensitivity to overhead lighting (especially fluorescent lights), and a feeling of being attacked when touched, particularly by light or sudden contact. Individuals may also experience discomfort or aversion to certain fabrics against their skin, nausea triggered by smells that are not unpleasant to most people, difficulty maintaining eye contact, and severe intolerance to certain foods due to their taste, texture, or temperature. Additionally, individuals may feel overwhelmed when exposed to multiple sensory stimuli simultaneously. It is important to note that sensory intolerance in this context does not necessarily reflect a refusal to engage with sensory stimuli but rather an inability to process the stimuli in any way other than as overwhelming or distressing. This often provokes a fight-or-flight response, a phenomenon also referred to as sensory overload. Sensory defensiveness varies between individuals. For example, one person may find high-pitched noises merely annoying, while another may experience physical pain from the same sounds. Similarly, one individual may be sensitive to the texture of mushy foods, while another may have difficulty with crunchy foods. Most individuals report significant issues with two or three senses, while experiencing milder difficulties with others. Causes The etiology of sensory defensiveness is believed to be multifactorial, involving genetic predispositions, environmental conditioning, substance abuse (such as drugs or alcohol), sexual abuse, or premature birth. Individuals diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) report higher-than-average rates of hypersensitivity to sensory stimuli. Effects and Treatment Sensory overload can lead to what is commonly referred to as a meltdown. This may manifest as behavior resembling a tantrum or as dissociation, where the individual withdraws into themselves. To cope with sensory difficulties, individuals often avoid situations that provoke irritation or distress. Occupational therapists frequently recommend sensory diets, which are personalized therapeutic interventions designed to expose individuals to calming sensory stimuli that help regulate their sensory systems. Controlled environments, such as Snoezelen rooms, are sometimes used to allow individuals to explore and manage sensory experiences in a safe and controlled manner. Many individuals also naturally develop their own calming sensory strategies, known as stims, which may include activities like listening to music, exercising, or engaging in other forms of pleasant sensory stimulation to reduce stress. Interestingly, some individuals report a heightened awareness of their senses under favorable conditions, which can be perceived as a positive aspect of their sensory sensitivity. These individuals often promote the use of stims or sensory diets as natural methods for stress reduction. Component of Other Disorders Sensory defensiveness is a subset of sensory integration dysfunction, which is itself considered a symptom of the autism spectrum. However, a person does not need to exhibit other autistic traits to experience sensory defensiveness or sensory integration dysfunction. These conditions are also commonly associated with developmental dyspraxia, cerebral palsy, and fetal alcohol syndrome.
